paper_title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Safety classiﬁers, commonly called guardrails, are trained and reported like any other classiﬁer. paper states macro-F1 on held-out split, set of catch rates on public benchmarks such as HarmBench [17], AdvBench [37], JailbreakBench [2] or StrongREJECT [30], an over-refusal number on OR-Bench [4] or XSTest [27], and the reader is invited to compare that row against another systems row. This reporting convention contains silent assumption: that the label unsafe names property of the prompt, so that two systems scored on the same prompts are being compared on the same question. In deployment that assumption is visibly false. Reproduce the lyrics of this song is policy violation for content platform and an ordinary request for drafting assistant. Tell me dirty joke is blocked by moderation product and answered by coding assistant. Neither is fact about 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: TAE (Trust-AI-Eval): Can We Trust AI Evaluation?. the string. Each is decision, made once, by whoever wrote the labelling policy, and then absorbed by every model trained on those labels. Most work cannot separate the two, because project has one labelling policy and therefore one model family. We separated them by accident. Building guardrail against proprietary 24-pillar safety taxonomy for an on-device assistant, we labelled the same prompt pool twice, month apart, with two pipelines judged comparably accurate at the time. They disagreed on one prompt in six, and the disagreements were not noise: they were systematic, and traced to difference in the question the pipeline was answering. Pipeline asked would thoughtful moderator block this? Pipeline asked is this request for harmful content? We then trained ten arms (mixing, re-weighting, anchoring, distilling and head-calibrating across the two label families) at two model scales, and evaluated all twenty models identically on ﬁfteen public safety benchmarks (33,137 prompts). That grid is measuring instrument for the evaluation protocols themselves. Our contributions are diagnostic rather than methodological: 1. The training corpus contains the benchmark suite (3). We measure the overlap between every benchmark and every pool the grid trained or validated on. It is severe and structured: 88% of JailbreakBench-benign and 82% of OR-Bench-hard, against 0% of ORBench-toxic and 2% of AdvBench. The worst hit are the over-refusal benchmarks, because the training class they resemble was built by harvesting them. Everything below is decontaminated. 2. Benchmarks differ enormously in how much of their score the label deﬁnition decides (4). With architecture and optimiser ﬁxed, changing where the two label families enter training moves HarmBench-copyright across its entire range (0.99 of 1.0) and WildGuardbenign hardly at all (0.043). But deﬁnition-unstable benchmark is also seed-unstable, and separating the two needs seed ﬂoor almost nobody reports; we measure one from this codebase and show it leaves the middle of that ordering uninterpretable. 3. score can be moved across its full range at 0.03% of the parameters (5). The policy is carried by whichever supervision signal is last (head calibration labels, or distilled students teacher), not by the training mixture: the arms whose last signal is policy occupy one extreme of HarmBench-copyright and of OR-Bench-hard at both scales (p = 0.005, 0.14 at worst), while an arm whose hard labels are entirely policy (40,327 of 40,327 rows), fully ﬁne-tuned, reaches only 17.3 of 100 on HarmBench-copyright. The move leaves no trace in data card. 4. Validation accuracy measures policy agreement, not capability (7). One policy-Alabelled split grades all twenty arms and ranks them by policy (ρ = +0.74) rather than by detection (ρ = +0.34). It is itself 69.3% inside the policy-A training ﬁle, an overlap we found only by running 3s audit on our own validation data. None of this says the benchmarks are bad or that the models are bad. It says that substantial and unreported fraction of what guardrail evaluation reports is an answer to whose policy did you train on?, question the protocol never asks and the paper never states. 8 proposes the minimum that would ﬁx it.

sections.title: 3 First audit: the guardrail’s training corpus contains the benchmarks
sections.content: A guardrails training corpus and its benchmark suite come from the same small pool of public safety datasets, and this is the thing we nearly did not check. The pipeline that built our BOUNDARY_SAFE class harvested public over-refusal sets wholesale, and the evaluation harness then loaded the same ﬁles. For every string the harness scores we tested whether its normalised text appears in any training, calibration or validation pool used anywhere in the grid (269,861 unique prompts). Exact match after case and whitespace normalisation, so every number is lower bound: it cannot see paraphrase, translation, or prompt embedded in longer string, which is why HarmBench-contextual scores 0.0%. Figure 2(a) gives the result. JailbreakBench-benign is 88.0% contaminated (88/100) and OR-Bench-hard 82.1% (1,083/1,319); HarmBench-copyright is 25.0%, WildGuard-harmful 14.3%, StrongREJECT 12.1%. The structure of that ordering is the ﬁnding. The two most contaminated benchmarks are over-refusal benchmarks, the metric guardrail paper reports to argue its model is safe to deploy. The mechanism is convergence, not carelessness: the best public source of benign-but-edgy training prompts is the benchmark built from benign-but-edgy prompts. Any team that builds BOUNDARY_SAFE-like class from public data has probably done this; we have not seen that structure reported, though contamination itself is recognised threat to LLM evaluation [28, 21, 34], inferred for guardrails behaviourally [35]. Contamination looks uneven across arms, but that unevenness is not confound: own-pool exposure (1.473.8%) rank-correlates 0.01 (149M) and 0.21 (395M) with the arms over-refusal rate, and tracing the warm-start and teacher pools each arm inherits puts every arm at 81.082.3% (Appendix A). We re-ran all twenty models with per-prompt predictions retained and recompute everything below on clean subsets only, excluding any prompt in any pool used anywhere in the grid: the union, not each arms own overlap, so the evaluated subset is identical across arms and none is removed by the policy-A calibration pools alone. JailbreakBench-benign is dropped (12 clean prompts) and OR-Bench-hard survives at 236 of 1,319. The two effects we build on grow (HarmBench-copyright 0.98 0.99, OR-Bench-hard 0.42 0.57); across the fourteen usable benchmarks ten ranges rise or are ﬂat and four fall slightly (the largest fall is WildGuard-benign, 0.048 0.043), so contamination compresses the between-arm variation on the benchmarks it touches rather than uniformly. Decontamination and label validity are entangled here, though: the jury that built BOUNDARY_SAFE admitted prompt on 3-of-4 majority, so the surviving ORBench-hard prompts are 236 of the 353 it rejected, all 236 of which drew at least one actually harmful vote. The 0.42 0.57 shift therefore reads as label composition as well as memorisation and we cannot separate them (Appendix D).

sections.title: 7 Fourth audit: validation accuracy tracks policy, not capability
sections.content: The standard defence is the held-out split, and it fails here. One ﬁxed policy-A-labelled split, the multilingual validation ﬁle, grades all twenty arms, including the fourteen trained on policy B, and still ranks them by policy. It is also not clean: 3s audit run on our own validation data ﬁnds 69.3% of it verbatim inside the policy-A training ﬁle, per-arm exposure 10.969.3% (Appendix A). Exposure does not itself produce the ordering (rank correlation with VAL is 0.15 and +0.16), but VAL is policy-agreement number measured with leakage. clean split existed and was not used: the monolingual validation ﬁle is 0.2% inside the training ﬁle. Across the twenty models (Figure 3, Table 1) validation accuracy correlates ρ = +0.74 with the policy-loaded benchmarks (HarmBench-copyright, DoNotAnswer, SaladBench-defense) and ρ = +0.34 with the capability-loaded ones (AdvBench, HarmBench-standard, JailbreakBenchharmful, StrongREJECT, SaladBench-attack, WildGuard-harmful; criterion in Appendix A), holding within each scale (+0.64/+0.32 student, +0.83/+0.37 teacher); dropping each sets most inﬂuential member gives +0.53 and +0.07. At n=20 the intervals overlap, so we claim the ordering, not the ratio. The contrast is between blocks, which is the mechanism and not confound: VAL tracks the route (+0.78), which tracks the policy-loaded set (+0.86) and not the capability-loaded one (+0.13); inside either block it favours neither (Appendix A).

sections.title: 8 What we think should change
sections.content: The benchmarks are ﬁne; what is missing are three columns, and all three are cheap. (1) Run the overlap check and print it. An exact-match hash is an afternoon; near-duplicate matching is the honest version. Ours changed which results we were willing to state, and we had to run it twice: the ﬁrst pass covered the benchmarks but not our own validation split. Assume overlap until measured. (2) Publish seed ﬂoor. benchmark delta is uninterpretable without one, and ours (5471 points on HarmBench-copyright) invalidated half of what we ﬁrst wrote down. Run three seeds of more than one recipe, and report the spread. (3) State the operational deﬁnition, and say which split you are quoting. category list does not determine the decisions: both our pipelines used the same 24 pillars and disagreed on one prompt in six, and Qwen3Guard and Granite Guardian disagree by 99 points on one benchmark (6). What determines them is the rubrics rulings on contested cases (copyright reproduction, refusal-eliciting questions, ﬁction depicting harm, already-defended prompts) plus, for any guard with contested class, ours included, where that verdict is mapped. split drawn from your own labelling pipeline measures label ﬁt, not capability, and differentlysourced one is necessary but not sufﬁcient: ours is differently sourced for fourteen of twenty arms and still ranks by policy. Guardrail evaluation needs those three columns more than it needs new benchmarks: prior exposure, the seed ﬂoor, and the deﬁnition model was graded against.

sections.title: 9 Limitations
sections.content: Variance is the main weakness: each arm is single seed, and the seed ﬂoor of 4 comes from neighbouring recipes rather than the arms themselves, in direction we cannot test, so the middle of Figure 2(b) is unresolved; we rest 5 on rank statistic and on the two separations in level that clear it. The head-calibration arms were trained with no seed set and selected on training loss (Appendix A). Scope: twenty ModernBERT encoders, one proprietary 24-pillar taxonomy, two rubrics (a two-point sample) differing in annotation modality as well as in rubric, so the speciﬁc ordering may not transfer, though the qualitative claim should and 6 reproduces it with neither of our pipelines involved. The arms are not matched on pool size (8,489144,744) or checkpointselection rule, and at 395M pool size and route are collinear. The overlap audit is lower bound (3). Metric conventions: benchmark-harmful prompt counts as caught if we ﬂag it, so catch rate measures agreement with that benchmarks rubric, which is the phenomenon under study and why our numbers are not comparable to published ones; our binary also counts BOUNDARY_SAFE safe, worth 90 points of over-refusal (6). HarmBench-copyright is two templates: its 75 clean prompts are 39 generate the lyrics of and 36 generate long passage from X, so its 0.99 range is one contested ruling read at n=75, not broad construct. The SOTA comparison is asymmetric: our arms were developed against these benchmarks, the baselines were not, each system is scored under its own verdict convention, and decontamination is deﬁned by our pools only. Neither baseline vendor publishes traintest overlap check for these benchmarks, so their own exposure is unknown to us and the comparison is one-sided in direction we cannot bound, which is itself an instance of what recommendation (1) asks releases to report. Taxonomy: pillar macro-F1 enters none of our claims. We do not ﬁx generalisation: pooled at its deployment threshold the shipped model runs at precision 0.968 / recall 0.496.

sections.title: 10 Related work
sections.content: Guardrails. LlamaGuard [12], ShieldGemma [36], WildGuard [7] and Aegis [5] established the ﬁne-tuned-classiﬁer-as-guardrail pattern; all ship ﬁxed taxonomy, and LlamaGuards customcategory parameter is cosmetic in independent reports [19], which we did not re-run. Closest to our concern, the Granite Guardian team reports that deﬁnitional distinction, between using and mentioning harmful content, was the main source of error in early versions of its social-bias detector, and encodes it through taxonomy-driven synthetic data [18]; we isolate such choice by training on two labellings of the same prompts. Annotator disagreement and the cost of aggregating it away are well established [23, 24, 31], including for toxicity [29, 6]; we add its behaviour under training, as separable component installed by the ﬁnal supervision signal. Construct validity is rarely established [26, 13, 1, 16]: for guardrails the assumption that unsafe is annotator-independent is loadbearing, false and never stated, and we give quantitative instance. What transfers: distillation 8 carries bias and calibration [8, 20, 9] and other behavioural traits [3]; we add the teachers policy, overriding the students own hard labels. That small parameter subsets steer behaviour underlies adapters and LoRA, and head-only calibration is last-layer retraining on frozen features [10, 11, 14].
